title: Grammar in Use: Tenses, Passive, Reported Speech and More
summary: Tenses (including present perfect and past progressive), active and passive verb forms, direct and reported speech, subject-verb agreement, comparatives and superlatives, if-sentences, standard English, formal and informal language and proofreading.

blocks.text: 1. Grammar in Checkpoint 6: what you need

This page covers the grammar you **use** every time you write and the verb forms the reading questions can ask you to **recognise**. In both **Paper 1 (Non-fiction)** and **Paper 2 (Fiction)**, Section A Reading is worth 25 marks and Section B Writing is worth 25 marks.

rows: A tick-one question can ask you to choose the **verb form** of a highlighted verb, for example **simple past passive** or **present perfect passive**, or to find a **passive verb** in the text.
You may be asked to find or explain a **comparative adjective** (*bigger, more dangerous*) in the text.

**Grammar and punctuation (7 marks)**: correct tenses, correct agreement, standard English and a range of verb forms. **Vocabulary and language (3 marks)**: the right level of formality for your audience.

blocks.title: Exam words
items: **Tense**: the form of a verb that shows **when** something happens (past, present, future).
**Base form**: the verb with nothing added: *go, eat, play*.
**Past participle** (3rd form): *gone, eaten, played*. Used after *have/has/had* and in the passive.
**Auxiliary (helping) verb**: *be, have, do, will, can...* used with the main verb.
**Progressive** (also called continuous): a form with *be + -ing* (*is running, was running*).
**Perfect**: a form with *have/has/had + past participle* (*has finished, had finished*).

blocks.text: 2. Tenses: the main forms

rows: She is walking to school now.
now, at the moment, today, this week
finished actions at a known past time
She was walking to school when it started to rain.
an action in progress in the past, often interrupted by a shorter action
while, when, at 8 o'clock last night
She has walked to school every day this term.
past actions connected to now / experiences / recent actions / unfinished time
ever, never, just, already, yet, since, for
She had already left when I phoned.
an action that happened **before** another past action
will + base form / am/is/are going to + base form
She will walk. / She is going to walk.
She has been walking for an hour.
an action that started in the past and is still going on

blocks.text: 3. Past simple and past progressive together

In stories (Paper 2) you will use these two tenses all the time. The **past progressive** sets the scene or shows a longer action; the **past simple** shows the short action that happens in the middle of it.

items: *I **was reading** in bed when the lights **went** out.* (long action + short interrupting action)
*While we **were eating** dinner, the phone **rang**.*
*The sun **was shining** and the birds **were singing**.* (setting the scene)

blocks.title: While or when?
blocks.text: Use **while** before the long action (past progressive) and **when** before the short action (past simple): *While I was walking, I saw a fox.* / *I was walking when I saw a fox.*
4. Present perfect or past simple?

rows: No finished time: *I **have visited** Luxor.* (at some time in my life)
Finished time is given: *I **visited** Luxor **last summer**.*
Result now: *I **have lost** my key.* (I still can't find it)
Just the past event: *I **lost** my key yesterday, but I found it.*
Unfinished time: *We **have lived** here **since** 2019 / **for** five years.*
Finished time: *We **lived** in Giza **for** five years.* (we don't now)

blocks.title: Never mix them
blocks.text: Do not use the present perfect with a finished time word: *I have seen him yesterday* ✗ → *I saw him yesterday* ✓
5. Irregular verbs you must spell correctly
6. Keep your tense consistent

Choose one main tense for your writing and **stay in it**. Most stories, recounts, diaries and news reports are written in the **past**. Information texts, reviews and persuasive texts are mostly in the **present**. Changing tense by mistake is one of the most common errors.

rows: *We arrived at the beach and Dad sets up the umbrella.*
*We arrived at the beach and Dad set up the umbrella.*
*Suddenly the door opens and a man walked in.*
*Suddenly the door opened and a man walked in.*

blocks.text: 7. Active and passive
In an **active** sentence, the subject **does** the action. In a **passive** sentence, the subject **receives** the action, and the doer moves to the end after **by**, or disappears.

items: **Active:** *The children **painted** the wall.* (the children do the action)
**Passive:** *The wall **was painted** by the children.* (the wall receives the action)
**Passive with no doer:** *The wall **was painted** last week.*

blocks.text: **How to recognise a passive verb:** look for a form of **be** + a **past participle**: *is made, was found, were taken, has been opened, have been sold, will be built.*
**How to change active into passive (steps):**

items: Take the **object** of the active sentence and make it the **subject**.
Add the correct form of **be**, in the **same tense** as the active verb.
Add the **past participle** of the main verb.
Add **by + the doer** only if it is important.

rows: The council **has opened** a new park.
A new park **has been opened** (by the council).

blocks.title: The two forms most often asked about
items: **Simple past passive** = **was / were + past participle**: *was found, were taken, was built, were invited*.
**Present perfect passive** = **has / have + been + past participle**: *has been found, have been taken, has been built*.
To tell them apart, look for **been**. If you see *has been / have been* + past participle, it is present perfect passive.

blocks.text: **Why do writers use the passive?** Learn these answers:

items: to focus on the **thing** or the **action**, not on who did it (*The pyramids were built over 4,000 years ago.*)
because the doer is **unknown** (*My phone was stolen.*)
because the doer is **obvious** or **not important** (*The thief was arrested.* We know it was the police.)
to make the writing sound **formal** and **factual**, as in reports, news reports and science texts
in stories: to hide who did something, which creates **mystery** (*The window had been smashed.*)

blocks.title: Worked example (tick-one style)
blocks.text: *Text: ...the old lighthouse **has been repaired** and will open again in June.* Which verb form is the highlighted verb? **A** simple past passive **B** present perfect passive **C** present progressive **D** past perfect. **Answer: B**, because it is *has been* + the past participle *repaired*.
8. Direct and reported speech

**Direct speech** gives the speaker's exact words inside inverted commas. **Reported speech** (also called indirect speech) tells us what someone said **without** their exact words and **without** inverted commas. Reported speech is very useful in **news reports**, recounts and stories.

items: **Direct:** *Hana said, “I am tired.”*
**Reported:** *Hana said (that) she was tired.*

blocks.text: **Four steps to change direct speech into reported speech:**

items: **Remove the inverted commas.** You can add *that* (it is optional).
**Change the pronouns** to fit who is speaking: *I → he/she, we → they, my → his/her, our → their*.
**Move the tense one step back** if the reporting verb is in the past (*said, told, asked*).
**Change time and place words** if needed.

rows: past simple: He said he **played** chess.
past progressive: She said she **was reading**.
past perfect: He said he **had finished**.
past perfect: She said she **had seen** a fox.
had to: He said he **had to go**.
the day before / the previous day
the next day / the following day

blocks.text: **Questions and commands:**

items: Yes/no question: *“Are you ready?” he asked.* → *He asked **if (whether)** I **was** ready.*
Wh- question: *“Where do you live?” she asked.* → *She asked where I **lived**.* (no question mark, normal word order)
Command: *“Sit down,” the teacher said.* → *The teacher **told** us **to sit** down.*
Negative command: *“Don't run!” Mum said.* → *Mum told us **not to run**.*

blocks.title: No backshift needed
blocks.text: If the reporting verb is in the present (*says, tells*), the tense does not change: *Ali says, “I am hungry.”* → *Ali says he is hungry.* The tense also usually stays the same for facts that are always true: *She said the Nile flows north.*

blocks.title: Use different reporting verbs
blocks.text: Instead of *said* every time, choose a verb that shows how something was said: *explained, replied, admitted, promised, warned, suggested, insisted, complained, whispered, announced*. This also helps your **Vocabulary and language** mark.
9. Subject-verb agreement
The verb must **agree** with its subject: a **singular** subject takes a **singular** verb, and a **plural** subject takes a **plural** verb.

rows: Singular subject → singular verb (+s in the present)
*either ... or / neither ... nor* → the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject
Neither the teacher nor the students **were** ready. / Either the students or the teacher **is** coming.
*everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, each, every* → singular
Everyone **is** here. / Each child **has** a book.
The real subject, not the nearest noun
The box of chocolates **is** on the table. (the box is)
One of my friends **lives** in Dubai.
There **is** a cat. / There **are** many shops.
Collective nouns (team, family, class) usually singular
Amounts of time, money and distance as one unit → singular
Ten kilometres **is** a long way to walk.

blocks.title: Mistakes the examiner sees every year
items: *we was* ✗ → *we were* ✓
*he don't* ✗ → *he doesn't* ✓
*there was many people* ✗ → *there were many people* ✓
*everyone have* ✗ → *everyone has* ✓
*the information were* ✗ → *the information was* ✓

blocks.text: 10. Comparatives and superlatives
A **comparative** compares **two** things (*taller than*). A **superlative** compares **three or more** and shows the top or bottom (*the tallest*).

rows: one vowel + one consonant: big, hot, thin
the biggest, the hottest, the thinnest
the happiest, the busiest, the easiest
long (most two syllables, all three or more): careful, beautiful, dangerous
the most careful, the most dangerous
the best, the worst, the furthest/farthest

items: Comparative: *The Nile is **longer than** the Thames.*
Superlative: *The Nile is **the longest** river in Africa.*
With *as ... as*: *My bag is **as heavy as** yours.* / *not as heavy as*
Adverbs too: *She ran **faster** than me. / He spoke **more quietly** than before.*

blocks.title: Never double them
items: *more better* ✗ → *better* ✓
*the most fastest* ✗ → *the fastest* ✓
*more easier* ✗ → *easier* ✓
*badder* ✗ → *worse* ✓

blocks.text: **Fewer or less? Many or much?** Use **fewer** and **many** with things you can **count** (*fewer cars, many books*). Use **less** and **much** with things you **cannot count** (*less water, much noise*).

**Why do writers use comparatives and superlatives?** To compare things clearly, to show which is best or worst, to make something sound better than anything else in persuasive texts and adverts (*the most exciting ride in Egypt*), and to give a clear judgement in reviews.
11. If-sentences (conditionals)
If-sentences talk about a **condition** and its **result**. They are not usually asked about directly in the reading questions, but you must use them correctly in your writing.

rows: If you heat ice, it melts.
If + present simple, will + base form
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If + past simple, would + base form
If I had wings, I would fly to the moon.
If + had + past participle, would have + past participle
If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: *If it will rain, we will stay home* ✗ → *If it rains, we will stay home* ✓ (no *will* after *if*)
*If I would be rich...* ✗ → *If I were rich...* ✓
When the *if*-clause comes first, put a comma after it. When it comes second, no comma: *We will stay home if it rains.*

blocks.text: **Where they help your writing:** persuasive texts (*If we do nothing, our beaches will disappear.*), instructions and advice (*If the water boils, turn down the heat.*), balanced arguments (*If the centre were built here, traffic would increase.*) and stories (a character's thoughts: *If only I had listened...*).
12. Standard English

**Standard English** is the correct, accepted form of English used in writing, school and the exam. Some forms are fine when chatting with friends, but they are **non-standard** and lose marks in writing (except inside a character's speech in a story, where they can show how the character talks).

rows: I did my homework. / I have done my homework.
Me and Adam went to the park.
Adam and I went to the park.
I didn't do anything. / I did nothing.
Everyone should bring their book if they wants.
Everyone should bring their book if they want to.

blocks.title: Me and I
blocks.text: Take the other person away and test: *Adam and I went* → *I went* ✓ (*me went* ✗). *The teacher thanked Adam and me* → *thanked me* ✓.
13. Formal and informal language
Your **audience** and **purpose** decide how formal you should be. Choosing the right level is part of **Vocabulary and language** and **Creation of texts** in the writing mark scheme.

rows: letters to a head teacher, council or company / reports / news reports / balanced arguments / information texts
emails and letters to friends or family / diaries / blogs for children / speech in stories
no: *do not, I am, it is*
precise, polite words: *receive, purchase, assist, require*
used often: *It has been decided that...*
exclamation marks and questions to sound friendly
We can't wait to see the new library!
We are looking forward to visiting the new library.
Loads of kids think the playground is rubbish.
Many pupils feel that the playground needs improvement.
Can you tell me when it opens?
Could you please inform me of the opening times?
We got lots of help from the teachers.
We received a great deal of support from our teachers.

blocks.title: مستوى اللغة والقواعد
items: قبل الكتابة اسأل: لمن أكتب؟ إذا كنت أكتب لمدير أو مسؤول، أو أكتب تقريرًا = لغة رسمية بدون اختصارات (don't / I'm).
إذا كنت أكتب لصديق أو أكتب يوميات = لغة غير رسمية، والاختصارات والأسئلة وعلامات التعجب مقبولة.
اختر زمنًا رئيسيًا واحدًا والتزم به. القصة والتقرير الصحفي = ماضٍ غالبًا.

blocks.text: 14. Proofreading: the last few minutes

Proofreading means reading your writing again to **find and fix mistakes** in grammar, spelling and punctuation. Leave **the last few minutes** of your 30 minutes of writing time for it. Check in this order:

items: **Sentences:** every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with . ? or ! (no comma splices or run-ons).
**Tense:** the same main tense all the way through.
**Agreement:** *we were, he doesn't, there are, everyone has*.
**Standard English:** no *we was, could of, me and him went*.
**Punctuation:** commas in lists and after opening clauses, speech punctuated correctly, apostrophes in the right place (*its/it's, their/they're/there*).
**Spelling:** check tricky words, especially irregular past forms and *-er/-est* spellings.

blocks.text: **Worked example.** This original paragraph has **at least ten** mistakes. Try to find them before you look at the correction.
*last saturday me and my cousin goes to the zoo, we was very excited. The lions was sleeping but the monkeys were the most funniest animals there. Their was a sign that said “dont feed the animals.”*

**Corrected:** *Last Saturday, my cousin and I went to the zoo. We were very excited. The lions were sleeping, but the monkeys were the funniest animals there. There was a sign that said, “Don't feed the animals.”*

items: *last* → *Last* (capital at the start of a sentence)
*saturday* → *Saturday* (days need capitals)
*me and my cousin* → *my cousin and I* (standard English)
*goes* → *went* (past tense)
*zoo, we* → *zoo. We* (comma splice fixed)
*we was* → *we were* (agreement)
*The lions was* → *The lions were* (agreement)
*the most funniest* → *the funniest* (double superlative)
*Their was* → *There was* (homophone)
*dont feed* → *Don't feed* (apostrophe for omission, and a capital letter at the start of the speech)
*said “* → *said, “* (a comma before the speech)

blocks.text: 15. Practice A: tenses

items.q: Complete: *While I ______ (walk) home, I ______ (find) a wallet.*
items.a: *While I **was walking** home, I **found** a wallet.* (past progressive + past simple)

items.q: Complete: *I ______ (never / see) snow.*
items.a: *I **have never seen** snow.* (present perfect: life experience)

items.q: Correct the mistake: *We have gone to Alexandria last summer.*
items.a: *We **went** to Alexandria last summer.* (finished time → past simple)

items.q: Complete: *By the time we arrived, the film ______ (start).*
items.a: *the film **had started**.* (past perfect: it happened before we arrived)

items.q: Which tense? *They are planting trees in the park this week.*
items.a: **Present progressive** (am/is/are + -ing).

blocks.text: 16. Practice B: active and passive

items.q: Active or passive? *The letter was delivered this morning.*
items.a: **Passive**: *was* + past participle *delivered*.

items.q: Which verb form is it? *Three new classrooms have been built.*
items.a: **Present perfect passive** (*have been* + past participle).

items.q: Which verb form is it? *The winners were chosen by the judges.*
items.a: **Simple past passive** (*were* + past participle).

items.q: Change to passive: *A strong wind knocked down the tree.*
items.a: *The tree was knocked down by a strong wind.*

items.q: Change to passive (no doer needed): *Someone has broken the window.*
items.a: *The window has been broken.*

items.q: Why does a news report say *A man has been rescued from the river* and not name the rescuers?
items.a: The passive focuses on the man and the rescue, which is the important news; it also sounds formal and factual.

blocks.text: 17. Practice C: reported speech

items.q: Report it: *“I am going to the market,” said Mum.*
items.a: *Mum said (that) she was going to the market.*

items.q: Report it: *“We have finished the project,” the boys said.*
items.a: *The boys said (that) they had finished the project.*

items.q: Report it: *“Will you help me tomorrow?” Ali asked his brother.*
items.a: *Ali asked his brother if (whether) he would help him the next day.*

items.q: Report it: *“Don't touch the oven!” Grandma told us.*
items.a: *Grandma told us not to touch the oven.*

items.q: Change to direct speech: *The coach said that the match had been cancelled.*
items.a: *The coach said, “The match has been cancelled.”*

blocks.text: 18. Practice D: agreement, comparatives, standard English and formality

items.q: Choose: *Neither my brother nor my sisters (like / likes) fish.*
items.a: **like**: the verb agrees with the nearer subject, *sisters* (plural).

items.q: Choose: *Each of the players (has / have) a shirt.*
items.a: **has**: *each* is singular.

items.q: Correct: *This is the most best day of my life.*
items.a: *This is **the best** day of my life.*

items.q: Write the comparative of *busy* and the superlative of *thin*.
items.a: *busier* and *the thinnest*.

items.q: Correct: *There is less people here than yesterday.*
items.a: *There **are fewer** people here than yesterday.* (people are countable and plural)

items.q: Correct: *If it will snow, we will build a snowman.*
items.a: *If it **snows**, we will build a snowman.*

items.q: Make formal: *The new sports hall is awesome and loads of kids use it.*
items.a: *The new sports hall is excellent, and many pupils use it every day.*

items.q: Correct all the non-standard English: *Me and Hassan done the washing up but we was tired.*
items.a: *Hassan and I did the washing-up, but we were tired.*

blocks.title: خلاصة الصفحة
items: المبني للمجهول = be + التصريف الثالث. إذا وجدت been بعد has/have فهو present perfect passive، وإذا وجدت was/were فقط فهو simple past passive.
في الكلام المنقول: احذف علامات التنصيص، غيّر الضمائر، ارجع بالزمن خطوة للخلف، وغيّر كلمات الزمان والمكان.
راجع في آخر 3 أو 4 دقائق: الحروف الكبيرة، النقط، الزمن، توافق الفاعل مع الفعل، والإملاء.
